newsitem.title: UK: SOCCER-SHIVERING COSTA RICANS RESPOND TO DERBY'S WARMTH".
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-SHIVERING COSTA RICANS RESPOND TO DERBY'S WARMTH".

text.p: Derby, an unremarkable city in the English midlands, seemed an unlikely destination for the premier league's latest foreign imports.
Costa Ricans Paulo Cesar Wanchope and Mauricio Solis knew almost nobody in England when they arrived in March, they had never been to Derby and they spoke only a few words of English.
But one month on, the pair have taken a shine to Derby.
"It's a lovely city, the people are very special, very helpful and they make you feel very much at home," Wanchope said. "It may be cold in England sometimes but there's a lot of human warmth here."
Wanchope has already created a little heat of his own during his first month in England.
He made his premier league debut at Manchester United's daunting Old Trafford stadium and celebrated by scoring one of the goals of the season to help Derby to an improbable 3-2 victory.

The tall striker collected the ball in his own half and surged goalwards, shrugging off challenges as he went. As four defenders closed in, he slid the ball under goalkeeper Peter Schmeichel into the corner of the United net.
"Whenever I score I feel great," the 20-year-old said at the club's training ground.
"But that was really a special goal, not only because it was my first for Derby or because it came in my first match, but because it was against one of the top clubs in Europe on their own ground."

Wanchope and Solis are the only Costa Ricans playing professionally outside the Spanish-speaking world and they have a certain curiosity value in a league more accustomed to imports from Eastern Europe and Scandinavia.
But while Wanchope's goal ensured him a spate of newspaper headlines, his friend and team mate Solis has made a less spectacular start to life in England.
The 24-year-old midfielder made his debut two weeks ago and is competing for a regular first-team place at Derby, who are heading for a mid-table end to their first season back in the top flight.
As a midfielder, he says he has found the pace and directness of the English game a challenge.
"The ball moves very quickly from defence to attack and hardly touches the midfield," Solis said.

"In Latin American football there are more touches in each move, more crossfield passes. Here the ball moves form defence to attack and then 'Goal!'. There's more physical contact and it's very different.
"But we're adapting to it. We were told about English football before we came and we saw it on television in Costa Rica so we knew what to expect."
Although they have settled at Derby, where they have signed three-year contracts, both Wanchope and Solis would like to go on to play for one of the giants of European soccer.

"Our first aim is to establish ourselves at Derby and take them as high as we can... but it's important to be ambitious and to have big ideas and we'd like to go on to play for a bigger side," Solis acknowledged.
"If we got the chance in the future to go to a bigger club in England then that would be perfect. But if not then maybe a club in another country."
Wanchope is equally ambitious.
"You always have to try to do better than you have done before. If this year we can help Derby finish in the top 10, next year we should be trying to help them get into the top five.
"The better the team is, the more interest from outside there will be in us."

At the end of the English league season Wanchope and Solis will return to Latin America to help a fast-improving Costa Rica side in the Copa America in Bolivia and in their bid to qualify for only their second World Cup finals.

The little Central American country, who conquered Scotland and Sweden to reach the last 16 of the 1990 World Cup, have twice beaten the United States and held regional giants Mexico to a goalless draw in their qualifying matches for France 98.
They also beat Cameroon 5-0 in a friendly in San Jose in March thanks in large part to a Wanchope hat-trick.

"Costa Rica have improved a lot in the last few years," Solis said. "The progress of the youth team has been an important factor. And it's good for players back home to see we're here and we're playing at the highest level."
